events.title: Everything I Want to Do In a Show | A One Woman Show
events.summary: Hi, I'm Heather Sejnow. You may remember me from such things as that Christmas Commercial for a toy store that gets played every year near St. Claire Shores; hosting shows at the Senate or Redford Theatre as dead celebrities or film characters; or living in Chicago for a short while to do Second City, iO, and then hop back to Detroit to perform at Go Comedy and Planet Ant. I've even nabbed the title of the only female stand up impressionist in the state of Michigan ( that I know of) . I haven't been on a real theatrical performance stage in a while and I'm about to turn 40. So for my mid-life crisis I'm putting on a show of "Everything I Want to Do in a Show". It's campy, crazy, and heartfelt. Most importantly, it's a love letter to everyone I've met and all the vessels of creativity I've learned along the way. Oh! And it's interactive, NSFW, and there will be some prizes for attendees. So come join me on a wild ride filled with puppets, impressions, burlesque, song, dance, and even Shakespeare. It's definitely... "Everything". Recommended for audiences 18+

events.title: Saturday Morning Physics | The Physics of Art and the Art of Physics
events.summary: Hybrid Lecture: Join us in Weiser Hall in person (Rooms 170 and 182) or stream live:https://myumi.ch/Z87k9 At the same moment Monet was painting the shimmering atmosphere, Rayleigh was explaining its physics. Moving from light and color through Helmholtz’s science of perception, this talk traces the remarkable journey from physical reality to what the eye sees, what the artist creates, and what the audience imagines—while discussing the physics principles behind it. It then turns the lens around to ask how beauty, elegance, and symmetry guide physicists in their search for the laws of nature.

events.title: Math Grad Show and Tell Seminar: A mathematical introduction to knitting
events.summary: Suppose you want a nice two-dimensional surface, but only have some one-dimensional string. Is all hope lost? Or could you entwine your string with itself in a way that approximates the surface you dream of? Good news: knitting’s got your back! And all you need to do is pull some loops through other loops. Knitted fabrics are breathable, flexible, and easy to construct either by hand or with a machine. They can stretch to about double their length without lengthening the constituent yarn. Knits are so popular that you are probably wearing one right now! In this talk, we will learn how knitted textiles are constructed and explore topological models of knitting. We will learn what it means to be knittable and meet a new knitted stitch that physicists designed to be less prone to unraveling than standard knitting. You will also get to practice knitting a few stitches for yourself!

events.title: Kristen Yeon-Ji Yun, cello & Phoenix Park-Kim, piano
events.summary: Duo Dolce presents an all-American program celebrating 250 years of American music, featuring works by composers including George Gershwin, Amy Beach, and Aaron Copland, alongside music shaped by immigrant and multicultural experiences. Together, these works create an American mosaic that reflects the country’s diverse cultural heritage, voices, and musical traditions. PROGRAM Antonín Dvorák: *Silent Woods op. 68 no. 5* (1891) Aaron Copland: *Old American Songs* (1952) - *Simple Gifts*, *I Bought Me a Cat*, *At the River* Harry Bulow: *Taegeuk* for solo cello (2024) Allen McCullough: Trilogette for solo cello (2025) - *Homage - J.S.B.*, *Night Song*, *Perpetuum Mobile* Erich Korngold: Romance Impromptu in E-flat major op. posth. (1946) Chen-Yi: Romance of Hsiao and Ch’in (1995) George Gershwin (arr. Ka-Wai Yu): Three Preludes (1926) - *Allegro ben ritmato e deciso*, *Andante con moto e poco rubato*, *Allegro ben ritmato e deciso* William Grant Still: *Summerland* (1935) Elliott Bark: *An-Nyoung: Goodbye/Hello* for cello and piano (2026) Amy Beach: Romance, Op.23 (1893) ABOUT THE GUEST ARTISTS KRISTEN YEON-JI YUN is a Clinical Professor in the Department of Music in the Patti and Rusty Rueff School of Design, Art, and Performance at Purdue University. She is an active soloist, chamber musician, scholar, and clinician. She has toured internationally, performing and giving master classes in countries including Malaysia, Mexico, Spain, France, Germany, and Taiwan. Her CD *Summerland* has received excellent reviews from *New Classics UK* and *American Record Guide* and was broadcast nationwide by major radio stations such as WQXR, WCNY, WBAA, and NPR’s *Sonatas and Soundscapes*. She earned her Doctor of Music degree in cello performance in 2012 from the Indiana University Jacobs School of Music, where she studied with the world-renowned cellist János Starker. Yun plays a 1766 Guersan cello. PHOENIX PARK-KIM, Professor of Piano at Indiana Wesleyan University, has performed throughout the United States and internationally across Asia, Europe, and Latin America. A prizewinner in numerous competitions, she has appeared as a soloist with orchestras including the Korean Philharmonic and Atlantida Orchestra (Spain), performing concertos by Bach, Mozart, Beethoven, Chopin, Rachmaninoff, Hummel, and Florence Price. A passionate advocate for African-American composers, she has received a Lilly Research Grant and special congressional recognition. Dr. Park-Kim is a sought-after clinician and adjudicator whose students have earned regional and national honors, including MTNA National Competition finalist placements.

events.title: Jia Yi Gu & Kate Yeh Chiu
events.summary: Material Feast Material Feast is an interdisciplinary dialogue featuring designers and practitioners interrogating the contemporary role of materials in design. Framed as a “feast,” a term that gestures toward sensory abundance, the event invites us to consider materials as processes rather than products. Designers Brittanie Dabney, Catie Newell, Meredith Miller, Melanie McClintock, and Ana Morcillo Pallarés will each give a brief presentation of their practice, using provisional objects and material samples to probe the boundaries between art, science, design, and craft. Alongside the presentations, a material library will bring together samples drawn from automotive plastic waste streams, quagga mussels from lake systems, and waste glass, as well as perforated textiles, hydrogels, and brittle sponges made from foraged “kin” species. Organized by Material Acts Material Feast is organized by Material Acts (Kate Yeh Chiu, Jia Yi Gu and Hilary Huckins-Weidner), a research platform exploring materials as cultural technique through public events centering an experimental library. The project attends to the logistical, economic, and technological actions that transform matter into the material substrate for our lives. Initiated in 2021 as part of Getty PST ART, the project has taken the form of a major exhibition at Craft Contemporary, an editorial project with e-flux Architecture, and a publication of ideas, conversations, and material inquiries. Working through exhibitions, programming, and editorial projects, Material Acts brings together theoretical and practical engagements with materials, addressing how design and architecture are entangled with social and ecological concerns. www.materialacts.org Contributors Brittanie Dabney Brittanie Dabney is the founder and CEO of Ecosphere Organics, a Detroit-based company that converts food waste from local restaurants and suppliers into reusable materials. An environmental scientist trained at Wayne State University, she studied microplastic pollution, and her company now develops compostable packaging and plant-based leather alternatives at Newlab. She is adjunct faculty at the College for Creative Studies and served on the 2025 Detroit Month of Design curatorial committee. Catie Newell Catie Newell is Professor of Architecture at the University of Michigan's Taubman College, which she joined in 2009 as the Oberdick Fellow. She is the founding principal of Alibi Studio, established in Detroit in 2010, and her work explores materiality in relation to place through material systems, light, and darkness. She is a Lucas Fellow, a Kresge Artist Fellow, and a Fellow of the American Academy in Rome. Meredith Miller Meredith Miller is Associate Professor of Architecture and Director of the Master of Architecture program at Taubman College. She holds a BS from the University of Virginia and a Master of Architecture from Princeton. With Thom Moran, she leads Post Rock, a research initiative developing a composite building product from waste plastics, and she is a founding member of the practice T+E+A+M. Melanie McClintock Melanie McClintock is Chair of Color & Materials Design at the College for Creative Studies, with an MFA from CCS and a BFA in Fashion Design from Virginia Commonwealth University. A CMF designer, multi-media artist, curator, and educator, she explores material-driven concepts of time, worthiness, and a sense of place. She worked in the fashion industry for over two decades in the United States, Qatar, and Indonesia. Ana Morcillo Pallarés Ana Morcillo Pallarés is an architect, designer, and researcher and Associate Professor of Architecture at Taubman College, teaching architectural design, design research, and spatial politics. She holds a PhD in architecture from Taubman and is developing research on the natural thermal properties of the biomatter of the quagga mussel as an opportunity for the fabrication of alternative by-products for the architectural residential industry. She is principal of Rumor Studio, formerly Morcillo Pallarés + Rule Arquitectos.

events.title: The Tree of Eternity
events.summary: The Tree of Eternity is an immersive, interactive installation that explores remembrance, loss, and the enduring presence of those we have loved. The installation centers on a projected tree surrounded by interactive terminal pods that control its structure. Visitors approach interactive pods positioned throughout the gallery space, where they are invited to recall memories of people or experiences throughout their lives. Depending on the kiosk they interact with, different effects will be present on the projected tree. As more visitors’ memories are inputted, the tree’s visuals adapt and change form, demonstrating that our memories persist with us. Projection mapping creates ethereal visuals accompanied by atmospheric audio. Even when visitors aren't actively engaging with the kiosks, the system generates ambient transmissions, suggesting that the tree—and the memories it embodies—continues to live and grow. The installation creates a dialogue between life and death, presence and absence, individual memory and collective remembrance, inviting participants to contribute to a living memorial that persists beyond any single moment of grief or reflection.

legacySeriesKeys: "don't let the sun": chamber choir & university choir|hill auditorium
events.title: "Don't Let The Sun": Chamber Choir & University Choir
events.summary: WORLD PREMIERE Composer Theodore Wiprud and librettist Richard Wesley have created an oratorio examining a widespread expression of racism in America, documented in the landmark book *Sundown Towns* by the late sociologist and historian James Loewen. Conducted by Director of University Choirs Eugene Rogers, *Don’t Let the Sun*, for chorus, vocal soloists, and orchestra, will run approximately 90 minutes (plus intermission). It tells the story of “sundown towns” where residents drove out or actively excluded specific groups from residing there (from being in a town after sunset) through ordinances, signs, and acts of violence. Sundown towns excluded Black people, and in some cases, Chinese Americans, Jewish people, Native Americans, Latinas/os and other racialized groups. Since the 19th century these towns have been prevalent throughout the U.S. and especially in the Midwest, West, and East. These policies did not completely disappear over time. The attitudes that drove them morphed into housing “covenants,” redlining, discrimination within the post-war FHA and discrimination in the granting of bank loans. The results of these decisions and policies haunt our country to this very day. *Don’t Let the Sun* will shine a light on this difficult chapter in America’s ever-expanding history, and help audiences engage productively with “hard” histories. Mr. Loewen’s *Sundown Towns: A Hidden Dimension of American Racism* is the definitive history of these phenomena. Another source is the “History and Social Justice” website launched by Dr. Loewen, which has had nearly one million visitors over the last three years, and continues to amass cases and first-hand accounts. Librettist Richard Wesley’s text is inspired by the voices of individuals impacted by sundown towns and more recent policies, examining the harm experienced by both the excluded and the excluders; and recent efforts by many sundown towns to reckon with their past and shape a better future. CONTENT ADVISORY: This program explores the difficult history of sundown towns in America, including themes of racial discrimination, antisemitism, exclusion, and historical language that some audience members may find disturbing. *"Don't Let the Sun" was commissioned with support from an Arts Initiative Project Support (AIPS) grant, an Arts Research: Incubation and Acceleration (ARIA) grant, the U-M Brehm Choral Commissioning Fund and generous support from the Department of History, the Department of American Culture, and the School of Music, Theatre & Dance.* ––– *Parking / Traffic alert for attendees:* https://smtd.umich.edu/2026-construction ABOUT THE GUEST ARTISTS THEODORE WIPRUD is a composer, an educator, and a researcher on the musical community’s work toward equity and inclusion. Many of his works address social issues, including vocal works like *American Journal* (Robert Hayden) and *A Georgia Song* (Maya Angelou); and orchestral works like his Violin Concerto *“Katrina”; Wind of Many Voices*, responding to the troubled history of South Dakota; and a second Violin Concerto *“on the brink”* exploring climate grief and climate action. RICHARD WESLEY is a playwright and screenwriter whose many plays deal with social-historical moments. He wrote the libretto for Anthony Davis’ Pulitzer Prize-winning opera *Central Park Five*. Mr. Wesley has received numerous awards including the NAACP Image Award for Best Picture (for *Uptown Saturday Night*) and the National Black Theater Festival’s August Wilson Playwright Award. He teaches at New York University.

events.title: Austin Zhu, carillon
events.summary: Economics graduate student Austin Zhu performs on the Charles Baird Carillon, an instrument of 53 bronze bells located inside the Burton Memorial Tower. The largest bell, which strikes the hour, weighs 12 tons, while the smallest bell, 4½ octaves above, weighs just 15 pounds. Thirty-minute recitals are performed on the Charles Baird Carillon at noon every weekday that classes are in session, followed by visitor Q&A with the carillonist. The bell chamber may be accessed via a combination of elevator and stairs. Take the elevator to the highest floor possible (floor 8), and then climb two flights of stairs (39 steps) to the bell chamber (floor 10). Hearing protection earmuffs are provided for visitors. Be prepared to walk on ice and snow in the bell chamber during winter. Built in 1936, the Charles Baird Carillon is not ADA accessible. Visitors with mobility concerns are invited to visit the Lurie Carillon.

events.summary: Experience a curated experience of the imaginary, featuring a lightly sci-fi, magnificent work of art--the LRCCS Fortune and Longevity Dragon, a 25-ft long, Asian-inspired full-body dragon sculpture for use in the traditional "dragon dance" crafted by renowned international artist Zhen Guo with U-M faculty arts lecturer Raymond Wetzel, artist Jeri Rosenberg, students, and volunteers The exhibition highlights the story of the dragon's fabrication and its impact on community.. An iconic symbol of inclusivity, strength, and courage, this newly imagined U-M dragon, with its futuristic flair, technological creativity and sustainable materials, invites students and the entire community to re-envision a classic cultural symbol for contemporary times. Presented by the Lieberthal-Rogel Center for Chinese Studies. This project was made possible by grants from the University of Michigan Arts Initiative and the Office of the Provost, Global Engagement. Additional funding was provided by ArtsEngine, Center for World Performance Studies, Stearns Collection of Musical Instruments, and U.S. Department of Education. With support from Asian Languages and Cultures, International Institute, James and Anne Duderstadt Center, Nam Center for Korean Studies, Residential College, School of Kinesiology, School of Music, Theatre & Dance, Taubman College, University of Michigan Library, University of Michigan Museum of Art, and Women’s and Gender Studies Department. *If there is anything we can do to make this event accessible to you, please contact us at cstep@umich.edu. events.title: Kathleen Beck, carillon
events.summary: Kathleen Beck performs on the Charles Baird Carillon, an instrument of 53 bronze bells located inside the Burton Memorial Tower. The largest bell, which strikes the hour, weighs 12 tons, while the smallest bell, 4½ octaves above, weighs just 15 pounds. Thirty-minute recitals are performed on the Charles Baird Carillon at noon every weekday that classes are in session, followed by visitor Q&A with the carillonist. The bell chamber may be accessed via a combination of elevator and stairs. Take the elevator to the highest floor possible (floor 8), and then climb two flights of stairs (39 steps) to the bell chamber (floor 10). Hearing protection earmuffs are provided for visitors. Be prepared to walk on ice and snow in the bell chamber during winter. Built in 1936, the Charles Baird Carillon is not ADA accessible. Visitors with mobility concerns are invited to visit the Lurie Carillon.

events.title: The Tree of Eternity
events.summary: The Tree of Eternity is an immersive, interactive installation that explores remembrance, loss, and the enduring presence of those we have loved. The installation centers on a projected tree surrounded by interactive terminal pods that control its structure. Visitors approach interactive pods positioned throughout the gallery space, where they are invited to recall memories of people or experiences throughout their lives. Depending on the kiosk they interact with, different effects will be present on the projected tree. As more visitors’ memories are inputted, the tree’s visuals adapt and change form, demonstrating that our memories persist with us. Projection mapping creates ethereal visuals accompanied by atmospheric audio. Even when visitors aren't actively engaging with the kiosks, the system generates ambient transmissions, suggesting that the tree—and the memories it embodies—continues to live and grow. The installation creates a dialogue between life and death, presence and absence, individual memory and collective remembrance, inviting participants to contribute to a living memorial that persists beyond any single moment of grief or reflection.

featuredEvents.experienceId: experience:["ann arbor","weiser hall","saturday morning physics the physics of art and the art of physics"]
featuredEvents.title: Saturday Morning Physics | The Physics of Art and the Art of Physics
featuredEvents.summary: Explore the intersection of physics and art in this hybrid lecture. Discover how scientific principles influence artistic creation and how beauty guides scientific discovery, featuring insights from a U-M Physics and Engineering professor.

evidence.description: Moving from light and color through Helmholtz’s science of perception, this talk traces the remarkable journey from physical reality to what the eye sees, what the artist creates, and what the audience imagines—while discussing the physics principles behind it. It then turns the lens around to ask how beauty, elegance, and symmetry guide physicists in their search for the laws of nature.

featuredEvents.experienceId: experience:["ann arbor","east hall","math grad show and tell seminar a mathematical introduction to knitting"]
featuredEvents.title: Math Grad Show and Tell Seminar: A mathematical introduction to knitting
featuredEvents.summary: Explore the mathematical underpinnings of knitting in this engaging seminar. Learn how knitted fabrics are constructed, delve into topological models, and discover a new stitch designed by physicists. Participants can even practice knitting a few stitches.

evidence.description: In this talk, we will learn how knitted textiles are constructed and explore topological models of knitting. We will learn what it means to be knittable and meet a new knitted stitch that physicists designed to be less prone to unraveling than standard knitting. You will also get to practice knitting a few stitches for yourself!

featuredEvents.summary: Experience an all-American program by Duo Dolce, featuring cello and piano works by composers like Gershwin, Beach, and Copland. This concert celebrates diverse cultural heritage and musical traditions, reflecting the country's rich mosaic of voices.

evidence.description: Duo Dolce presents an all-American program celebrating 250 years of American music, featuring works by composers including George Gershwin, Amy Beach, and Aaron Copland, alongside music shaped by immigrant and multicultural experiences. Together, these works create an American mosaic that reflects the country’s diverse cultural heritage, voices, and musical traditions.

featuredEvents.title: Riders in the Sky
featuredEvents.summary: Experience the legendary Riders in the Sky as they bring their award-winning harmonies, Western wit, and high-yodeling adventures to The Ark. This iconic group celebrates the heritage of Western music with both classic and original tunes.

evidence.description: What began as a celebration of classic Western Music and an evening of hilarity has become a career, and that career has become a legend, one which, 40 years on, shows no signs of stopping or even slowing down much.
